title: A Letter to a Young Head of Department
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau writes as an experienced educator offering advice to a new middle leader — a head of department navigating the institutional politics, relational complexity, and intellectual demands of leading a team within a school. The letter form is deliberate: it allows for the personal, direct voice of a mentor rather than the prescriptive tone of management literature. Didau advises the young HOD to maintain professional skepticism toward school initiatives that come from above, to build genuine relationships with teachers in the department rather than relying on positional authority, and to keep student outcomes — not adult comfort — as the constant reference point for every decision. The letter touches on the particular challenge of middle leadership: occupying a position that has real responsibility for instructional quality but limited formal authority to enforce change, which means influence and trust must do the work that power cannot. Didau also addresses the intellectual life of the HOD, encouraging them to stay genuinely curious about their subject and about pedagogy, because the credibility of a middle leader comes in significant part from visible engagement with ideas.
points: Middle leadership's defining challenge is responsibility without commensurate authority: HODs are accountable for departmental quality but must accomplish change through relationship and influence rather than positional power.

Maintaining professional skepticism toward whole-school initiatives is framed as a professional responsibility, not a rebellious posture: the HOD's job is to filter what reaches the classroom through the lens of what will actually serve students.

Keeping student outcomes — not adult convenience, not departmental harmony, not institutional loyalty — as the decision-making reference point is the hardest discipline of middle leadership precisely because the pressures to compromise it are constant.

Genuine curiosity about subject and pedagogy is not a luxury for a head of department; it is the primary source of the credibility that makes influence possible — teachers follow leaders who visibly love and study what they teach.

The letter form itself reflects a pedagogical choice: the most effective professional advice is personalized and relational, not prescriptive and generic — a principle that applies equally to how HODs should develop the teachers in their departments.
quotes: Over the past few months I’ve had a series of increasingly depressing series of encounters with heads of English seeking on advice and guidance on how to contend with senior leaders who seem intent on making their lives as hard as possible. The following letter represents both my frustration and despair as well as a repository of all the pearls of wisdom I’ve tried to share.

By serious, I don’t mean solemn — solemnity is frequently the counterfeit of thought — I mean that you must preserve an allegiance to reality. Line managers may prefer a fog of intentions, but you need to develop a taste for facts.

Better to say, “Last time we met, we agreed that behaviour support would be arranged before the end of the week. That hasn’t happened, so I need to know whether the support is still coming or whether I’m expected to manage this without it.” Separate motive from effect.

People do struggle, and humane leadership requires more than pointing at standards and relying on shame. But standards must always remain visible, otherwise support becomes a place to hide rather than a route back to doing the job properly.

But, as you well know, a lesson isn’t good because it comes on a slide deck packaged with approved ‘dual coded’ logos but because it causes students to know something worth knowing or do something worth doing. Architecture that enables this is useful anything that prevents it is an obstacle course arranged in front of a fire exit.

We all wanted to be trusted but to be trustworthy you must be honest. Over committing — promising what you’d like to happen but which you know is unrealistic — is always worse than disappointing people at the outset.
Compromise can be a form of cowardice but, when intelligently chosen, it’s not surrender. Of course, your school is not a salon convened for the satisfaction of your ideals.
